title: DFS on Lisbon: Street Intersections Explored ⚡
description: Watch DFS “dive” down one set of streets in Alfama before backtracking—exactly how depth first search traversal behaves on a graph. This real-map visualization turns intersections into nodes and streets into edges so you can see the call-stack logic move.
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps—what happens when DFS explores real city intersections ⚡

In this Lisbon (Alfama) visualization, every intersection becomes a node and every street segment becomes an edge. DFS follows one path as deep as it can, then backtracks when it hits a dead end—so the traversal order is all about the stack behavior.

How to recognize DFS mechanics:
• “Go deep” to the next unvisited neighbor
• Use recursion or an explicit stack
• Mark visited to prevent cycles

Takeaway: DFS is great for reachability and exploring connected components—but it’s not guaranteed to find the shortest route.

Debate question: If the goal is the quickest street route, should we use DFS at all—or switch to BFS / Dijkstra?
